Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

protest verb and noun

object loudly

also protests, in protest, outcry, cry out against

classical

Liv. 3.21.3: reclāmantibus cōnsulibus
Cic. Dom. 10: ab ūniversō senātū reclāmātum est (Lewis & Short)

reclāmō, reclāmāre, reclāmāvī, reclāmātum

intransitive; with the dative of what is protested (ōrātiōnī), often impersonal passive (reclāmātum est) or ablative absolute (reclāmantibus omnibus)

protest, cry out against

To shout against, contradict loudly: of a theatre, a senate, a whole province (Lewis & Short). The noun reclāmātiō is rare (Cic. Phil. 4.5).

Other words

  • intercessiō, intercessiōnis f. — a formal protest: a tribune’s veto

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Caes. BC 1.7 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 181: veto

    The tribune’s stepping in to block a decree or a law; to make it is intercēdere with the dative (Traupman 181). It also means going surety for someone (Lewis & Short).

  • prōtestor, prōtestārī, prōtestātus sum — declare publicly, bear witness

    avoid · post-classical · Quint. Decl. 4.21 (Lewis & Short)

    A false friend: post-Augustan, “declare, testify” (Lewis & Short), the older sense of English protest, not “object”.

Examples

  • tribūnī reclāmantibus cōnsulibus refectī

    the tribunes were re-elected over the consuls’ protestsLiv. 3.21.3

See also protest, mind, attack.

SourcesLewis & Short: reclamo · Lewis & Short: reclamatio · Lewis & Short: intercessio · Lewis & Short: protestor
